name: state
intent: Let an object alter its behaviour when its internal state changes by making each state a first-class object that the context delegates state-dependent requests to, so the object appears to change class.
problem: An object's behaviour depends on a state field and the resulting if/switch ladders spread the same state logic across every method; adding a state or a transition means editing every method, illegal state/event combinations are only discovered at runtime, and state-specific data and code cannot be tested or evolved independently.
context: Applies to an individual object (or a small object collaboration) whose state-dependent behaviour is spread across several operations and whose states are a finite, predetermined set: protocol and session state machines, order or document lifecycles, connection and device modes, workflow steps, and editors with modal behaviour. It pays off when the number of states and transitions is not small, when states carry their own data or collaborators, and when the state set is expected to grow; it is not a substitute for a persistent workflow engine or for an entity whose state is merely a database column.
benefits: State-specific behaviour is localised in one class or value per state, eliminating the fat conditionals that the state field otherwise forces into every method of the context.
Transition rules become explicit code instead of nested conditionals, so the legal state graph is visible and reviewable.
New states and new transitions arrive as new state classes or new transition entries; existing states stay closed for modification (open/closed principle at state granularity).
State objects can carry their own data and collaborators, which removes state-specific temporary fields from the context.
Contexts become small: they own the current state and the data every state needs, and delegate everything else.
States without instance data can be shared (one instance per state, e.g. enum members or singletons), so the per-object cost of a state machine is one reference.
tradeoffs: More classes or objects than an enum field plus a switch: for two or three states with one or two conditional methods the indirection costs more than it saves.
You must decide where transitions live; if concrete states instantiate each other, every state depends on its successors, producing a class graph that is harder to evolve and to test state by state.
State objects that need context data require a back-reference or a widened context interface, which leaks context internals into the state classes.

Every transition allocates or swaps an object unless states are shared instances, adding allocation and pointer chasing to what was a field write; negligible per event, visible when millions of small objects each run a state machine.

The current state must also exist outside the object (serialized, persisted, logged); the pattern says nothing about state identity, so a mapping between state objects and stable tokens has to be maintained by hand.
Debugging spans more frames: behaviour is found by chasing context, then state object, then method, and shared stateless state instances make stack traces look uniform across objects.
Concurrency is not addressed: a transition is a read-modify-write on the state reference, so concurrent events need external synchronisation or a single-threaded owner.

participants.responsibility: Defines the interface clients use, holds a reference to the current ConcreteState, delegates state-dependent requests to it, and offers the single sanctioned way to replace the current state.
Declares the interface for the behaviour associated with a state of the context: exactly those operations whose behaviour varies by state.
Implements one state's behaviour; may read the context through a back-reference and may initiate the transition to a successor state.
Uses the context through its ordinary interface and never sees state objects, state enums or transition tables.
In data-oriented realizations a declarative structure maps (state, event) pairs to a successor state and side effects, replacing per-state code with data that can be inspected and tested as a whole.

use_cases: Connection or protocol objects whose read/write/close behaviour differs between closed, connecting, established and closing states.
Order, invoice, ticket and document lifecycles (draft, review, approved, published, archived) with role-dependent transitions.
UI editors and media players with modal input behaviour (idle, playing, paused, locked) where the same gesture means different things per state.
Stateful protocol implementations in simulators and test harnesses where each phase must process the same events differently.
Game entity behaviour (patrol, chase, flee, dead) and device or gamepad modes driven by stimuli and timers.
Message-driven workflow steps where an incoming command or event triggers a step transition, often combined with a command handler or process manager.
Authentication and authorisation flows (login, multi-factor, token refresh, session revocation) where each step gates the next and invalid transitions represent security vulnerabilities.
Saga orchestrators and long-running distributed transactions where each saga step is a state with compensation actions on failure, persisting the current step across service restarts.
Lexer and parser engines where tokenisation state (start-of-token, inside-token, escaped) drives different character-handling rules; each grammar rule becomes a concrete state.
TCP, HTTP/2, TLS, or protocol handshakes where connection lifecycle states govern which messages are legal, expected, or malformed at each phase.
Bidirectional negotiation flows such as feature capability discovery, version handshakes, or encryption parameter agreement where both sides track shared state.
Embedded control systems and device mode machines (e.g., sleep/wake/active, sensor calibration states) where state violations can trigger hardware faults.
IoT device shadows and MQTT-enabled embedded systems where connection state, telemetry mode, and command processing are driven by explicit state machines with deterministic periodic tasks.
Payment and financial transaction flows (authorize → capture → settle → refund → dispute) where atomic transitions prevent race conditions and regulatory compliance requires auditable state history.
ML pipeline orchestration where data preparation, training, evaluation, and deployment stages are explicit states with guard conditions on transitions.
Kubernetes controller reconciliation loops where resource desired vs observed state drives apply, wait, or error sub-states per controller.
CDN edge caching where origin-fetch, cache-hit, and stale serving states govern request routing and header manipulation.

Erlang/OTP gen_statem implements this pattern as a standard OTP behaviour: a server process whose callback module handles events per state (state_functions mode, one callback named after each state) or via a single handle_event_function, returning {next_state, NextState, NewData, Actions} with state-enter hooks, state-owned timeouts, and event postponing - the production shape used for telecom and protocol processes (RabbitMQ, Ejabberd, WhatsApp backends).

The Linux kernel ships the data-driven variant of State in C: the FSM libraries (e.g. drivers/s390/net/fsm.c, drivers/isdn/mISDN) build a (state, event) -> action jump table from a declarative template via init_fsm/FsmNew, dispatch with fsm_event, and keep the current state in an atomic variable - table-driven State inside device drivers, with optional transition-history logging for debugging.
avoid_when: There are two or three states with one or two conditional methods: an enum field plus a switch, or a discriminated union plus match, is clearer and cheaper.
The choice is really about algorithm selection among independent, unaware strategies that never trigger transitions: that is Strategy, not State.
The state is a persisted business fact owned by a workflow engine or a database constraint: keep it on the aggregate or record and let the engine drive transitions.
The behaviour varies per request rather than per object lifetime, for example request-scoped mode flags: parameterise the operation instead of mutating object state.
You need compile-time proof that only certain operations are callable in certain states: use a typestate encoding or a generated state machine rather than runtime state objects.
anti_patterns: The state-as-literal context: a state field compared against string or integer literals in every method, with the transition logic duplicated next to each comparison.
God-state: one state class with a mode flag inside it, recreating the original conditionals one level down.
Transition anarchy: every state and every caller may assign the state field directly, so the legal state graph exists only in the developers' heads.
Using State where Strategy belongs: state objects that never transition and never know each other, selected per call by the client - an indirection layer with no behavioural benefit.
Persisting the state object or its class name instead of a stable token, so refactoring or renaming a state corrupts stored data.

State explosion without hierarchy: a flat state space where every combination of orthogonal concerns is a separate state class, leading to a transition graph that is large, duplication-heavy, and hard to review.

Typestate confusion: encoding state validity in types (typestate) but implementing it with runtime State objects, so the compile-time guarantees are lost and the runtime objects recreate the same conditionals they were meant to replace.
Silent transition failure: a transition method that returns early or no-ops when the (state, event) pair is illegal, making the illegal transition invisible at runtime and hard to diagnose.

Embedding protocol logic in state machines: treating a network protocol or workflow engine as a State pattern problem when the transitions and persistence model actually require a full finite-state machine framework (e.g., KAFKA consumer groups, BPMN engines).

Method-per-event interface at scale: every state must implement every event so most methods become throw-invalid-operation stubs, and adding one event edits the context interface plus every concrete state class (python-statemachine quantifies this: 4 states × 3 events = 12 method implementations, 9 of which throw exceptions).

Orthogonal concerns flattened into one machine: n independent dimensions produce n × m states with near-duplicate code (standing vs standing-armed vs jumping vs jumping-armed); the fix is parallel regions or separate machines, not more state classes.

Re-entrant cascades: a state's entry/exit action or guard drives another transition in place, so entry actions run twice, recursion is unbounded, or a deferred event loops forever; queue internal events and transition only after the current run-to-completion step.

In-memory state as authority for a distributed workflow: a restart forgets it, duplicated deliveries re-fire transitions, concurrent updates are lost, and there is no compensation path; durability, ordering and compensation belong to a persisted store, saga orchestrator, or durable workflow engine.

Server-side workflow bypass: trusting client-side state or step sequence rather than enforcing transitions server-side; attackers can skip steps, reorder requests, or replay state identifiers to reach unauthorized states (OWASP WSTG workflow bypass).

Concurrent Workflow Order Bypass (CWOB): distributed or multi-step workflows where final actions race ahead of prerequisite steps (e.g., payment before availability check) because transitions lack atomic guards; enforce all precondition checks atomically before the transition fires.
design_principles: Single responsibility per state: each concrete state owns one state's behaviour and its transition rules.
Open/closed principle: new states extend the state abstraction without modifying the context or existing states.
Separation of concerns: the state graph and transitions are decoupled from the client-visible context interface.
Polymorphism over conditionals: replace state tests with dispatch on the current state value.
Information hiding: clients never see state objects; the context owns the state reference and the transition policy.
Transition atomicity: every state change goes through exactly one sanctioned transition method that can validate preconditions, update the state reference, and fire side effects as a unit.
Stable token persistence: serialise a mapping-safe token (enum, string ID) rather than object identity or class references to survive refactoring and support versioning.
best_practices: Keep the state abstraction to the operations that actually vary and leave state-independent behaviour on the context.
Decide and document transition ownership: states drive transitions for tight state coupling, a transition table when the graph must be visible and testable as data.
Make the context the only writer of the state reference and route every change through a transition method that can validate the (state, event) pair.
Reuse one instance per stateless state; if instances are mutable, never share them across contexts.
Model persistence with a stable state token (enum or string) plus one mapping to state values.
Test the graph as a table of (state, event) to (successor state, effect) and cover illegal transitions, not just the happy path.
Fold new states into the abstraction instead of adding conditionals to existing states, and keep each state small enough to read in full.

Apply Interface Segregation to the State interface: keep it narrow (only the operations that vary) so concrete states never implement no-op stubs for irrelevant methods — a wide interface forces every state to couple with context internals.

Prefer a data-driven transition table (state × event → successor + effects) over code-driven transitions when the graph is large or must be reviewed by non-developers; a table is trivially testable and model-checkable.
Use guarded transitions (precondition checks on the context or event payload) to make illegal transitions explicit failures rather than silent no-ops or dropped events.

Model hierarchical/nested states for domains where states naturally cluster (e.g., Online + Offline each with sub-states); this keeps individual state classes small while preserving the full state space.

Validate illegal transitions in unit tests: for each (state, event) pair that should be rejected, assert that the context raises, returns an error, or stays in the original state — not just that the happy path works.

When the number of states grows beyond ~10 or the transition graph is dense, consider a formal formalism (statechart, FSM table, or XState) before hand-rolling individual state classes; the pattern's structure scales only so far without tooling.

Split orthogonal state dimensions into separate machines or parallel regions: n independent concerns produce n + m states instead of n × m; SCXML parallel regions and UML orthogonal regions formalise this decomposition.

Use explicit entry and exit actions on each state so setup and teardown run on every path into and out of the state, eliminating duplicated transition-side setup code; exit actions run innermost-first, entry actions outermost-first (SCXML 3.1.1 ordering normatively fixes this).

Process events run-to-completion on a single owner: one event at a time, each transition atomic, and any event raised during a step queued and handled after the step completes; this avoids re-entrancy and the ill-defined 'between two states' window.

Validate the machine statically in CI: every state reachable from initial, every non-final state has an exit, every (state, event) pair either transitions or is an explicitly documented no-op, and generate the diagram from the definition so it cannot drift.

Enforce transitions server-side: never trust the client to supply the current state or the step sequence; validate every transition against the authoritative server-side state before acting (OWASP Business Logic Security).
Use idempotency keys for non-idempotent transitions (e.g., payment capture) to safely retry on network failure without double-execution.

Profile before optimising: allocation-heavy transitions (GoF with make_unique) cost ~10–12 ns/transition in C++; if hot-path latency matters, evaluate enum+switch (zero allocations) or source-generated dispatch before rewriting all state objects.

Apply typestate for embedded or safety-critical code: encode valid state transitions in the type system (Rust lifetime/typestate, SPARK/Ada) so illegal operations are compile-time rejections rather than runtime exceptions.

Use EventStorming workshops to discover aggregate state machines before writing code: model domain events, commands, and state transitions collaboratively to find natural state boundaries and prevent state explosion.
Generate state diagrams from machine definitions in CI: keep diagrams and code in sync automatically so documentation never drifts from the implemented graph.

Boby and others, "State" — Game Programming Patterns (https://gameprogrammingpatterns.com/state.html): practical game-development perspective on finite state machines, hierarchical state patterns, and pushdown automata.

Adamczyk, "The Anthology of the Finite State Machine Design Patterns" — Hillside PLOP 2003 (https://hillside.net/plop/plop2003/Papers/Adamczyk-State-Machine.pdf): organises FSM patterns into three groups; foundational taxonomy of State pattern variants and extensions.

Khourshid, "Effective state machines for complex logic" — Effect Days 2024 / XState (https://github.com/statelyai/xstate): drives modern statechart practice (hierarchical, parallel, guarded transitions) in JavaScript/TypeScript; formalises the actor model for state machines.

Wikipedia, "Finite-state machine" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite-state_machine): formal FSM theory; UML state-machine extensions (orthogonal regions, hierarchical/nested states); relationship to automata-based programming.

vincehuston.org, "Behavioral Patterns – rules of thumb" (http://vincehuston.org/dp/behavioral_rules.html): concise State vs Strategy, Flyweight, Chain of Responsibility, Mediator distinctions drawn from GoF.

Harel, D., "Statecharts: A Visual Formalism for Complex Systems", Science of Computer Programming 8(3), 1987 — https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-6423(87)90035-9 — origin of hierarchical/orthogonal state decomposition; the formal answer to state explosion.

W3C, "State Chart XML (SCXML): State Machine Notation for Control Abstraction", W3C Recommendation, 1 Sept 2015 — https://www.w3.org/TR/scxml/ — normative semantics: onexit→transition→onentry ordering, compound-state transition lookup, parallel regions, run-to-completion, event-discard when no transition matches.

Garcia-Molina, H. & Salem, K., "Sagas", SIGMOD '87 — https://doi.org/10.1145/38713.38742 — long-lived transactions with compensation; formal basis for saga orchestrators and the idempotency requirement in distributed state machines.

Schneider, F. B., "Implementing Fault-Tolerant Services Using the State Machine Approach: A Tutorial", ACM Computing Surveys 22(4), 1990 — https://doi.org/10.1145/98163.98167 — replicated state machines; Agreement + Order requirements; t+1 vs 2t+1 replicas; commutable requests relax ordering.

Nystrom, R., "State" — Game Programming Patterns — https://gameprogrammingpatterns.com/state.html — richest practitioner source: enter/exit actions, orthogonal decomposition (n+m vs n×m states), hierarchical machines, pushdown automata, static vs instantiated state objects, FSM limits and when to use behaviour trees.

python-statemachine, "Coming from the State Pattern" — https://python-statemachine.readthedocs.io/en/v3.1.1/how-to/coming_from_state_pattern.html — per-item cost analysis: 4 states / 3 events = 12 method implementations, 9 of which throw exceptions; strict vs reactive event semantics; table-driven alternative.

Stately/XState docs, "What are state machines and statecharts?" — https://stately.ai/docs/state-machines-and-statecharts — modern statechart vocabulary: parent/atomic/parallel states, regions, initial/final states, self-transitions, guards, and the actor-model integration.

Martin Fowler, "Event Sourcing" — https://martinfowler.com/eaaDev/EventSourcing.html — state derived from an event sequence; complete rebuild, temporal query, replay; replay must suppress external effects.

Maglione, S., "State machines and Actors in XState v5" — https://www.sandromaglione.com/articles/state-machines-and-actors-in-xstate-v5 — project structure (context.ts, events.ts, actions.ts, machine.ts), async init via Input, actor invocation per state, inter-actor communication patterns.
Stately AI, "XState v5 Quick Start" — https://stately.ai/docs/quick-start — create machine, turn into actor, send events, delayed transitions, context, input, framework integration.

OWASP, "Business Logic Security Cheat Sheet" — https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Business_Logic_Security_Cheat_Sheet.html — server-side state machines, atomic transitions, idempotency keys, explicit per-step validation for multi-step workflows.

OWASP, "Testing for the Circumvention of Work Flows" (WSTG) — https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/latest/4-Web_Application_Security_Testing/10-Business_Logic_Testing/06-Testing_for_the_Circumvention_of_Work_Flows — workflow bypass via step skipping, request reordering, state replay; server-side enforcement required.

OWASP, "BLA2:2025 — Concurrent Workflow Order Bypass (CWOB)" — https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-for-business-logic-abuse/docs/the-top-10/workflow-order-bypass.html — race conditions in distributed/multi-step workflows; atomic guards required across all prerequisite checks.

Bug Bounty Playbook, "State Machine Bugs" — https://bugbounty.info/Attack-Surface/Web/Business-Logic/State-Machine — step skipping, state replay, out-of-order execution in multi-step flows (signup, checkout, password reset).

Comprehensive Rust (Google), "The Typestate Pattern" — https://google.github.io/comprehensive-rust/idiomatic/leveraging-the-type-system/typestate-pattern.html — enforce valid state transitions at compile time in Rust using type parameters and PhantomData; Serializer<S> example; self-consuming transitions prevent stale object reuse.

Willcrichton, "Typestate — Type-Driven API Design in Rust" — https://willcrichton.net/rust-api-type-patterns/typestate.html — ReadingFile/EofFile as distinct types; consuming ownership for transitions; PhantomData approach; compile-time enforcement of file API correctness.

Cliffle, "The Typestate Pattern in Rust" — https://cliffle.com/blog/rust-typestate/ — API visibility varies by state; consuming-style transitions prevent invalid state reuse; practical embedded systems examples.

Rust Embedded Book, "Typestate Programming" — https://rust-embedded.github.io/book/static-guarantees/typestate-programming.html — FooBuilder typestate for configure-before-use; compile-time enforcement on embedded devices.

rs4ts, "The Type-State Pattern" — https://rs4ts.dev/22-common-patterns/02-type-state/ — TypeScript runtime vs Rust compile-time state tracking; zero-cost abstraction comparison; builder pattern generalisation.

Lamport, "Model Checking TLA Specifications" — https://lamport.azurewebsites.net/pubs/yuanyu-model-checking.pdf — TLC model checker for TLA+; invariant verification over finite-state models derived from TLA+ specs; practical performance notes on cache-coherence protocol verification.

Akdağ et al., "TLA Verification of Cache-Coherence Protocols" — https://lamport.azurewebsites.net/pubs/fm99.pdf — TLC applied to FSM verification; symmetry breaking for state-space reduction (~50%); 3 days to 1 week per full run on symmetric multi-component systems.

Apalache, "The Symbolic Model Checker for TLA+" — https://apalache-mc.org/ — symbolic TLA+ model checker via SMT (Z3); bounded model checking, inductive verification, randomised symbolic execution; backend for Solarkraft/Atomkraft blockchain governance verification.

Brandolini, A., "Introducing EventStorming" — https://tonytvo.github.io/introducing-event-storming/ — model aggregates as state machines; domain events as state transitions; EventStorming discovers state boundaries and prevents state explosion before coding.

Morin, "Enhancing Business Logic with PlantUML and EventStorming" — https://dev.to/tmorin/enhancing-business-logics-with-plantuml-and-eventstorming-de0 — EventStorming + PlantUML for text-based, version-controlled state machine documentation; bmf-tech/plantuml-libs for EventStorming building blocks.

Farley, "Event Storm To Software Design" — https://spencerfarley.com/2024/02/01/event-storm-to-software-design/ — functional-core + event-driven model: business rules as pure functions returning domain events; centralised state management; avoiding stateful ports-and-adapters complexity.

Guzenfeld, P., "C++ State Machine, Three Ways: Switch/Case, GoF unique_ptr, and C++23 Variant — Benchmarked" — https://pavelguzenfeld.com/posts/cpp-state-pattern-switch-oop-variant-benchmarked/ — GoF (unique_ptr) costs ~50 ns/mission due to heap allocation (~10–12 ns/allocation, 4 per mission); switch/case ~0.74 ns/mission zero allocation; variant ~8.25 ns/mission; virtual dispatch overhead negligible when warm.

ZeroAlloc-Net, "ZeroAlloc.StateMachine" — https://github.com/ZeroAlloc-Net/ZeroAlloc.StateMachine — source-generated zero-allocation FSM for .NET via Roslyn; [StateMachine] attribute emits switch expression dispatch; benchmarks: ~36 ns vs ~4,495 ns (124x faster) vs Stateless 5.15; AOT/trimmer safe.

Eli Miller, "JVM Performance with State Pattern Optimizations" — https://notes.elimelt.com/systems/performance/efficiently-implementing-state-pattern-jvm — enum inline vs AtomicReference polymorphic on JVM; low contention: mixed results; high contention: CAS retries degrade polymorphic; results JVM-sensitive; proper JMH benchmarking recommended.

Akka, "Event Sourcing" — https://doc.akka.io/libraries/akka-core/2.10/typed/persistence.html — EventSourcedActor persists domain events (not raw state); recovery via event replay + optional snapshot; Effect.persist semantics; imperative vs mutable state within eventHandler.

Orleans, "Event Sourcing | dotnet/orleans" — https://deepwiki.com/dotnet/orleans/8.1-event-sourcing — JournaledGrain<TGrainState, TEventBase>; Confirmed state vs TentativeState; RaiseEvent → local event + persisted event; StateStorage vs LogStorage vs CustomStorage providers; multicluster consistency.

Akka vs Orleans comparison — https://github.com/akka/akka-meta/blob/master/ComparisonWithOrleans.md — Akka event-sourcing preserves business-meaningful event history; Orleans snapshot-per-grain is database-like; actor single-behaviour vs typed-grain interfaces; async/await + TPL integration in Orleans.

StateMQ — https://github.com/Thanos3G/StateMQ — deterministic state-machine framework for MQTT-enabled embedded systems; explicit states as small integers; fixed-period tasks; table-based MQTT event→state mapping; no dynamic memory; ESP-IDF + esp-mqtt.

vortexmakes, "MQTT-Reactive" — https://github.com/vortexmakes/MQTT-Reactive — non-blocking MQTT v3.1.1 client in C; active object + state machine; deferrable events; WaitingForNetConnection → WaitingForSync → Sync composite state; no blocking in core flow.

Erlang/OTP, "gen_statem" — https://www.erlang.org/doc/apps/stdlib/gen_statem.html — OTP's generic state-machine behaviour (replaces gen_fsm since OTP 20.0): state_functions vs handle_event_function callback modes, {next_state, NextState, NewData, Actions} transitions, state_enter hooks, state-owned timeouts, and postpone/retry of events a state cannot yet handle.

Linux kernel, finite-state machine library, drivers/s390/net/fsm.c — https://codebrowser.dev/linux/linux/drivers/s390/net/fsm.c.html — the data-driven State variant in production C: init_fsm builds a (state, event) → action jump table from a declarative template, fsm_event dispatches through it, the current state is an atomic variable, and optional history logging records transitions; the same shape appears in drivers/isdn/mISDN (FsmNew).

Cloudaffle, "Criticism and Caveats Of The State Design Pattern" — https://cloudaffle.com/series/behavioral-design-patterns/state-criticism/ — a dedicated misuse/criticism treatment: added classes and indirection outweigh benefits for simple cases; overkill for a few states and transitions; state-consistency management becomes hard as states/transitions grow; states that own their transitions become tightly coupled to successors; polymorphic dispatch costs more than plain conditionals.
